opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cost number got a lot of attention, and it's worth putting it in context. The figure people quoted, somewhere in the range of tens of dollars, comes from the fact that the actual fine-tuning run for s1 was very small. We took Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and did supervised fine-tuning on just 1,000 carefully selected examples, the s1K dataset, and that took about 26 minutes on 16 H100 GPUs. If you price that out at typical cloud rates, you get a very small number.

But I'd be careful not to read that as "you can build a frontier reasoning model for fifty dollars." That cost sits on top of a lot of prior investment. The base model, Qwen, was pretrained by a big team with an enormous compute budget. The reasoning traces we trained on were distilled from a strong existing reasoning model. And there was a lot of experimentation behind choosing those 1,000 examples: we started from a pool of around 59,000 questions and ablated different selection criteria, like difficulty, diversity, and quality, before settling on the final set. None of that shows up in the headline number.

So my interpretation is this: the low cost shows that a strong pretrained model already has much of the reasoning capability latent in it, and you don't need massive RL or millions of examples to unlock it. A small amount of high-quality data is enough to teach the model the format and behavior of extended reasoning. Then the other half of the paper, budget forcing, where we control how long the model thinks, for example by appending "Wait" when it tries to stop early, lets you trade test-time compute for accuracy.

The real takeaway is less "reasoning is cheap" and more "the marginal cost of eliciting reasoning from a good base model is surprisingly low." That matters for openness and reproducibility, because it means academic labs and smaller groups can study these test-time scaling behaviors without frontier-lab budgets.

r001.rationale: The response says the reasoning traces were distilled from a strong model and that this prior investment is not included in the headline cost.

r002.rationale: It mentions openness and reproducibility, but does not state that published datasets let others replicate the results using only the final training run.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the number that got a lot of attention was something like under fifty dollars in compute for the fine-tuning run, and I want to be careful about how that's interpreted. That figure is real, but it refers to a very specific thing: taking an existing, already very strong base model, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and doing supervised fine-tuning on just a thousand examples. That's about 26 minutes on 16 H100s. So the cheap part is the last mile, not the whole journey.

The reason it can be that cheap is that we're not teaching the model to reason from scratch. The base model already has those capabilities latent in it from pretraining and from whatever post-training Qwen did. What our thousand examples do is more like elicitation. We're showing the model the format of thinking for a long time before answering, and then budget forcing lets us control how long it thinks at test time. So you're nudging behavior, not building it. And nudging is cheap.

There's also the cost of the data itself, which doesn't show up in that number. We started from around 59,000 questions, generated reasoning traces with Gemini, and then filtered down to a thousand based on quality, difficulty, and diversity. That filtering turned out to matter a lot. If you just train on a random thousand, or even on the full 59k, you don't get much better, and sometimes worse on some measures. So the "cost" really includes the intellectual work of figuring out which examples to keep, plus the distillation from a stronger model.

So I'd say the right interpretation is: the marginal cost of unlocking test-time scaling behavior in a strong open model is now very low. That's a meaningful finding, especially for academic labs, because it means you can do serious research on reasoning without a huge budget. But it's not a claim that you can build a frontier reasoning model for fifty dollars. Someone paid for the pretraining, and someone paid for the model that generated the traces. We're standing on that.

r001.rationale: The response says the under-$50 figure covers only the fine-tuning run and excludes the cost of generating reasoning traces, which came from Gemini.

r002.rationale: The response describes the data and filtering process, but does not say the datasets were published or that others can replicate the results with only the final training run.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between the cost of the final fine-tuning run and the cost of creating the capabilities you’re starting from. S1 starts with an already pretrained model and fine-tunes it on a small set of reasoning examples from a much stronger model. So the low reported training cost is the incremental cost of that fine-tuning, not the cost of building the whole system from scratch. It doesn’t include the base model’s pretraining or all the work involved in generating and selecting the data.

That’s still exciting: it suggests you can elicit strong reasoning behavior with surprisingly little additional training. But there’s also inference cost. If you improve performance by letting the model think longer, you’re spending more compute at test time. So I’d interpret the result as evidence that a small, carefully chosen dataset can go a long way, rather than evidence that the entire capability was created for that low price.

r001.rationale: It says the low reported cost excludes the work involved in generating and selecting the training data.

r002.rationale: It does not say S1’s datasets are published or that others can replicate the results using only the final training run.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important to distinguish the cost of the final training run from the cost of producing the model overall. The roughly $6 figure is for fine-tuning on those 1,000 examples. We started from a strong pretrained model, and the examples contain reasoning traces generated by another very capable model. So a lot of computation and knowledge is already baked into both the starting model and the data.

The interesting result is that, with carefully selected examples, you can get a strong model to adopt this reasoning behavior very cheaply. It doesn’t mean we built all of those capabilities from scratch for $6.

r001.rationale: It identifies the roughly $6 as the cost of fine-tuning on the examples and notes that generating the reasoning traces required computation already baked into the data.

r002.rationale: It does not say that S1’s datasets were published or that others could use them to replicate the results with only the final training run.
